title: How a heavy steel ship floats
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: How can a metal ship float?
Why does a ship sit lower when it is loaded?

forces.label: Weight
forces.ask: Why doesn't the heavy steel sink?

explain.say: Steel is about eight times denser than water, so a solid lump of it sinks. Yet ships weighing many thousands of tonnes float easily.

draw.text: How a heavy steel ship floats

forces.label: Weight
forces.ask: Why doesn't the heavy steel sink?

explain.say: When a ship sits in water, it pushes some water aside. The water pushes back up with a force called upthrust, equal to the weight of the water pushed aside.

forces.label: Weight
forces.ask: Why doesn't the heavy steel sink?

explain.say: A ship's hull is a hollow shell full of air, so it is very big for its weight. It can push aside a lot of water without sinking deep.

forces.label: Weight
forces.ask: Why doesn't the heavy steel sink?

explain.say: The ship settles until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the ship. Then weight and upthrust balance, and it floats. Load it with cargo and it sits lower.

forces.label: Weight
forces.ask: Why doesn't the heavy steel sink?

faq.a: Upthrust, or buoyancy, is the upward push of a liquid or gas on something in it. It equals the weight of the fluid the object pushes aside, an idea first worked out by Archimedes.

faq.q: Why doesn't the heavy steel sink?
faq.a: Because the steel is shaped into a hollow hull full of air. The whole ship, steel plus the air inside, is less dense on average than water, so it can push aside its own weight of water while still sticking up above the surface.
asks: How can something made of metal float?

faq.q: Why does a ship sit lower when it is loaded?
faq.a: Extra cargo adds weight, so the ship sinks deeper until it pushes aside enough extra water to balance it. Marks on the hull, called load lines, show how deep it may safely sit.
If water gets into the hull, it replaces the air and the ship becomes much heavier for its size. Once it can no longer push aside its own weight of water, it sinks.
asks: Why do ships sink when they get a hole?

faq.q: Do ships float higher in salt water?
faq.a: Yes. Sea water is a little denser than fresh water, so a ship needs to push aside slightly less of it. A ship sailing from a river into the sea rises a little.
asks: Is it easier to float in the sea?

facts: Archimedes found over 2,200 years ago that the upthrust on an object equals the weight of fluid it pushes aside.
Steel is roughly 7.8 times as dense as water.
Load lines on a ship's hull, often called Plimsoll lines, show how deeply it may be loaded in different waters.

quiz.say: Why can a steel ship float when a steel nail sinks?

options.show: Its hollow hull pushes aside its own weight of water
options.say: Its hollow hull pushes aside its own weight of water

options.say: Ship steel is lighter than nail steel

quiz.why: The hollow, air-filled hull makes the ship big for its weight, so it displaces enough water to balance its weight before it sinks.

wrong.1: Steel is equally dense in both; the shape makes the difference.
wrong.2: A ship floats even with its engines switched off.
